text:
Lande c. Feldman

2026 QCCS 984

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTRÉal

No.:

500-17-136338-251

DATE:

March 24, 2026

_____________________________________________________________________

BY

THE HONOURABLE

LUC MORIN,
J.S.C.

_____________________________________________________________________

IRWIN LANDE

-and-

CLAUDE-ANDRÉE PION

Plaintiffs

v.

JOSEPH FELDMAN

-and-

KHADIJA EL HACHMI EL ALAOUI

Defendants

_____________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT
[1]

_____________________________________________________________________

I-

OVERVIEW

[
1
]

Plaintiffs seek the issuance of a
Mareva
order
against the Defendants. The same orders are sought in two separate files:

1.1.

First, in relation to the execution of a
judgment issued by the Honourable Justice Thomas Davis, S.C.J.
[2]
, against Defendant Joseph Feldman
[3]
, as
confirmed by the Court of Appeal
[4]
; and

1.2.

Second, in connection with a Paulian Action
instituted against Feldman
[5]
and his wife Khadija El Hachimi El Alaoui for the alleged
fraudulent transfer of assets
[6]
.

[
2
]

The two files are interconnected in that the
Paulian Action seeks to extend the Plaintiffs’ realization efforts arising from
the Davis Judgment to Defendant Alaoui, Feldman’s wife, who has received
significant transfers of assets from her husband.

[
3
]

Let us begin with the obvious: the factual
backdrop to this matter is unusual.

[
4
]

The Davis Judgment awarded approximately
$1.2M

to the Plaintiffs as a result of Feldman’s defamatory statements about their
lifestyle, which he claimed could only be sustained by their alleged possession
of gold stolen by the Nazis from Jewish victims during the Holocaust. Justice
Davis granted moral and punitive damages in light of Feldman’s repeated violations
of the Plaintiffs’ fundamental rights.

[
5
]

The Davis Judgment was rendered on June 16, 2025.
On November 14, 2025, the Court of Appeal granted the Plaintiffs’ Application
to dismiss Feldman’s appeal of the Davis Judgment, finding that
“the appeal,
on its face, has no reasonable chance of success.”
Although Feldman filed
an application for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada on January
13, 2026, the Davis Judgment is fully executable.

[
6
]

This forms the backdrop to the Plaintiffs’
present application seeking to implement a freeze on the Defendants’ assets
through a
Mareva
order.

[
7
]

For the reasons set out below, the Court is of
the view that the conditions warranting the issuance of a
Mareva
Order
are met with regard to the Paulian Action.

II-

ANALYSIS

[
8
]

Since the Court of Appeal’s decision in November
2025, Plaintiffs have attempted, painfully, to say the least, to execute the
Davis Judgment.

[
9
]

Feldman fled to Florida, and when he was
eventually located and served with a notice to be examined on his assets, he
reluctantly agreed to appear on March 18, 2026. Yet only days before the
scheduled examination, Feldman informed Plaintiffs’ attorneys that he would no
longer be available, citing a medical appointment and offering no alternative
dates.

[
10
]

In November 2025, Plaintiffs learned that
Feldman had transferred nearly
$3M
from one of his Canadian bank
accounts to his wife Alaoui’s bank account in Morocco.

[
11
]

This prompted the filing of the Paulian Action
against both Feldman and Alaoui. In that context, Alaoui was scheduled to be
examined on April 2, 2026, but on March 19, 2026, her attorney informed
Plaintiffs’ counsel that he could not confirm whether she would attend. In
fact, during today’s hearing, Alaoui’s attorney confirmed that she would not
attend her scheduled examination.

[
12
]

In March 2026, Plaintiffs further learned that
Feldman had assigned a
$1,6M
hypothecary claim on a property to his
wife.

[
13
]

The Plaintiffs’
Mareva
Application is
supported by allegations strongly indicating that Feldman is attempting to evade
his obligations under the Davis Judgment and to render himself judgment proof
by a series of undervalued transactions in favour of his wife.

[
14
]

Is it enough to warrant the extraordinary
issuance of a
Mareva
Order?

[
15
]

The Court believes so.

[
16
]

As the Court of Appeal noted in a recent case,
Giroux
v. Entreprises Bertrand Roberge ltée
[7]
, under Quebec law, the
Mareva
injunction is inspired by the
interlocutory injunction. The applicant must therefore demonstrate: (
i
)
a
prima facie
case, (
ii
) serious and irreparable harm, and (
iii
)
that the balance of convenience favours his position. Added to these criteria
is the requirement of urgency when the application is for a provisional-type
injunction, as it is in this case.

[
17
]

A
Mareva
order essentially constitutes
the
in personam
counterpart to the
in rem
nature of a pre‑judgment
seizure, which explains why, both measures are generally sought together.
Authors Piché‑Messier (now a colleague of this Court) and Bussières‑McNicoll
summarize the nature and purpose of this type of order as follows
[8]
:

L’ordonnance de type Mareva, aussi connue sous l’appellation de
« freezing order » en common law, est un ordre du tribunal commandant
à la partie défenderesse ou à une tierce partie, telle une institution
financière, de ne pas se départir d’actifs en possession pour toute période
précisée par le tribunal. Cette ordonnance, destinée à ne trouver application
que dans
des cas extrêmes, gèle entre les mains du possesseur certains
actifs appartenant à l’individu poursuivi
, et ce, si nécessaire
jusqu’au jugement final.

L’ordonnance de type Mareva, généralement obtenue ex
parte, vise à prévenir la dissipation ou le détournement d’actifs dans un
contexte de comportements frauduleux, louches, déloyaux ou de mauvaise foi
visant à rendre le jugement final inefficace
. Faisant échec au principe selon lequel la Cour
n’empêchera pas un défendeur de disposer de ses biens avant que les droits des
parties n’aient été établis, cette ordonnance ne s’applique que dans des
cas exceptionnels, faute de quoi elle est susceptible de donner lieu à des abus
graves.

[Emphasis added]

[
18
]

As the Court of Appeal stated in
Desjardins
Assurances générales inc. v. 9330‑8898 Québec inc.
[9]
, a
Mareva
injunction will only be granted where there is
convincing evidence of a real risk that assets may disappear, and only if it is
reasonable to fear that the defendant is seeking to thwart the execution of a
potential judgment by engaging in deceptive acts, such as concealing assets
from their patrimony, for example.

[
19
]

Exactly the case here.

[
20
]

The Court is satisfied that the criteria
justifying the issuance of a
Mareva
order at this provisional stage are
met, for the following reasons:

20.1.

Urgency

The November
2025 transfer of $3M and the March 2026 assignment of the $1,6M hypothecary
claim reveal a mounting series of measures taken by Feldman and his wife to
shield their assets from the Plaintiffs’ realization efforts.

Coupled with
their tepid cooperation regarding scheduled examinations, these actions present
a strong indication that they are maneuvering to complicate and frustrate the
Plaintiffs’ ability to realize on the Davis Judgment. Immediate judicial
intervention is therefore required in the circumstances.

20.2.

Appearance of Right

The Davis
Judgment clearly entitles the Plaintiffs to full satisfaction of their claim in
the approximate amount of $1.2M. This judgment is fully executable
notwithstanding the application for leave to appeal filed with the Supreme
Court of Canada.

There is a
strong appearance of right regarding the Paulian Action in light of the recent
transfers made by Feldman to his wife, after the Davis Judgement was rendered, leading
to the conclusion that he is trying to shield his assets and render himself
judgment proof with the help of his wife Alaoui.

20.3.

Irreparable Harm

A cursory
review of the allegations in the Plaintiffs’ Application, the Paulian Action,
and the Davis Judgment supports the Plaintiffs’ contention that the Defendants
are attempting to shield their assets and evade their obligation to pay the
$1.2M owed under the Davis Judgment.

The transfer
of assets and value beyond the reach of creditors constitutes irreparable harm,
as it may entirely defeat the Plaintiffs’ ability to realize on their judgment.

20.4.

Balance of Convenience

Absent a
Mareva order, the Plaintiffs may be left with assets that are effectively
unrecoverable.

By contrast,
the injunction will impose minimal prejudice on the Defendants. It will not
inhibit their ability to contest the Paulian Action. The draft order submitted
by the Plaintiffs provides for an allocation of $5,000 per month for living
expenses and a budget of $40,000 for legal fees.

Whether these
amounts are fully adequate remains to be determined, but the Court is satisfied
that proper safeguards have been put in place to avoid financially asphyxiating
the Defendants.

The Court
fully agrees with the Court of Appeal’s guidance in
Giroux v. Entreprises
Bertrand Roberge ltée
[10]
that courts must exercise caution and rigor before issuing a
Mareva
-type
order, especially when it may result in the financial paralysis of those
against whom it is pronounced. That said, this can be alleviated by providing
for a portion of the restrained assets to be allocated to Plaintiffs’ living
expenses or legal fees, as is the case here.

That said,
the Court remains of the view that at the renewal hearing, both Plaintiffs and
Defendants will have the opportunity to seek adjustments to these allocations
in keeping with the criteria established in the applicable case law.

In this
regard, the Court is mindful of the recent decision of the Ontario Superior
Court of Justice in
The Regional Municipality of Peel v. Dualeh
[11]
, which underscores that allocations for living and legal expenses
are not automatically granted in the context of a
Mareva
order.

This
decision, which is based on consistent Ontario case law dating back to the
Ontario Court of Appeal’s judgment in
Waxman v. Waxman
[12]
, essentially confirms that a defendant seeking an exceptional order
allowing him to draw on assets frozen by a
Mareva
injunction to cover
living expenses and legal fees bears the burden of establishing, on a balance
of probabilities, that:

•

The assets not covered by the
Mareva

injunction and still available to him are insufficient to meet his living
expenses and legal fees.

•

He has attempted to meet his living expenses and
legal fees from other sources.

•

The living expenses and legal fees to be
incurred are reasonable in the circumstances, having regard to the contemplated
means of defence in relation to the principal proceeding to which the
Mareva

relates.

•

The defendant is acting in good faith and has
provided full and frank disclosure of his true financial situation.

It bears recalling that the
Mareva
injunction is not a
civil law concept. It originates in English law and was later incorporated into
Canadian law as an exceptional tool designed to freeze existing assets to
prevent their dissipation before judgment.

It is therefore useful to
draw inspiration from precedents rendered in other jurisdictions, while keeping
in mind the dual nature of our civil law system.

The Court sees no reason,
however, why the criteria developed, and the approach adopted by the Ontario
courts would be incompatible with our civil law framework.

On the contrary, it must be
remembered that, despite the exceptional nature often associated with a
Mareva
order, it is
generally issued in very particular circumstances, namely where there is an
objective fear of asset dissipation and allegations of suspicious or dishonest
conduct going beyond mere civil fault, all of which may justify issuing the
order on an
ex parte
basis
.

[
21
]

The Court will therefore issue the Mareva order,
but
only
with respect of to the Paulian Action. Counsel for the
Plaintiffs candidly acknowledged that they were unable to identify any
motivated precedents in Quebec in which such orders were granted after a final
and executable judgment had already been rendered.

[
22
]

This is unsurprising, given the injunctive
nature of a Mareva order and its core objective, which is to preserve the
status
quo
between the parties until a final and executable judgment is issued. It
typically serves as a protective and conservative measure
en route
to
the ultimate adjudication of the litigation.

[
23
]

Finally, Plaintiffs’ attorneys argued that
article 657 C.C.P. empowers the Court to issue a post judgment
Mareva

order. It is a tempting argument; however, the Court does not share this view.

[
24
]

The powers conferred on the Court under article
657 C.C.P. must be exercised with caution. The stability of judgments and the
principle of res judicata should be set aside only in the presence of serious
circumstances. Article 657 C.C.P. does not authorize the Court to alter or
expand the substratum of a judgment.

[
25
]

Recently, in
Air Canada v. P.A.
[13]
, the Court of Appeal provided, in a single paragraph, a distilled
statement of the state of the law regarding the scope of the interpretative
power granted to the Court. Although this power must be interpreted broadly and
liberally, it cannot be misused to the point of becoming a blank cheque
amounting to judicial review, an appeal, or even a revocation. A decision
rendered under article 657 C.C.P. must be the “natural extension” of the
original order:

[20]      En conclusion, l’article 657
du
Code de procédure civile
permet au tribunal
d’interpréter
ou préciser
un jugement afin d’en
faciliter l’exécution
et
lui confère le pouvoir de déterminer les sommes auxquelles les parties ont
droit en application d’un jugement. Dans cette optique, « [l]a finalité de
l’article 657 du
Code de procédure civile
est de permettre la
résolution rapide d’une difficulté résultant de l’exécution d’un jugement sans
qu’il ne soit nécessaire d’enclencher un tout nouveau processus judiciaire avec
les délais et les coûts que cela comporte ».
La seule limite au
pouvoir du tribunal de rendre des ordonnances en vertu de cet article consiste
à ne pas modifier le jugement rendu
. En effet, une décision rendue en
vertu de l’article 657 doit s’inscrire dans le
prolongement naturel de la
décision précédente, il ne doit pas s’agir d’un moyen d’appel déguisé
.

[Emphasis added – references omitted]

[
26
]

Issuing, on an
ex parte
basis, an entire
set of conclusions grounded in post‑judgment conduct that was never
before the Court can hardly be characterized as a “natural extension” of the
original order.

[
27
]

In any event, the Court is of the view that the
Mareva

order sought, even if issued solely in the Paulian Action file, will fully achieve
the purpose the Plaintiffs are pursuing, namely to freeze the Defendants’
assets until the Paulian Action is adjudicated.

III-

CONCLUSION

[
28
]

The Court is satisfied that the
Mareva

order is appropriate and necessary under the circumstances.

[
29
]

A word on duration.
Ex parte
orders are
always delicate, as the Court hears only one side of the story. Given the far-reaching
scope of a
Mareva
order, the Court will issue it for a period of
30
days
only. This will allow the Defendants to present their version of
events and will permit the parties, as appropriate, to revisit the allocations
for living and legal expenses.

[
30
]

As for the sealing order requested in respect to
Exhibits R-6, R-22 and R-27, it is unsupported in the Plaintiffs’
Mareva

Application.

[
31
]

The Supreme Court’s guidance in
Sherman
(Estate) v. Donovan
[14]

reminds us that documents that are personal and sensitive may, in exceptional
circumstances, be the subject of a sealing order. Although mere embarrassment
caused by the disclosure of personal information in the context of public
judicial proceedings is not enough to justify limiting the open court
principle, there are circumstances in which an aspect of a person’s private
life takes on a clear public‑interest dimension.

[
32
]

A court may depart from the open court principle
when the disclosure of highly sensitive information seriously threatens a
person’s dignity. The issue is not simply the personal nature of the
information, but rather the degree of its sensitivity and the risk of harm to
dignity that society has an interest in protecting.

[
33
]

In short, when it comes to private information,
the threshold for setting aside the strong presumption in favour of open court
proceedings is high. The heavy burden of persuading the Court to depart from
this strong presumption rests on the Plaintiffs.

[
34
]

In the Court’s view, that high threshold is not
met here. There is nothing in the Plaintiff’s Application supporting this
request and it will therefore be denied.

FOR ALL
THESE REASONS, THE COURT:

[
35
]

GRANTS

Plaintiffs’ Application for the issuance of a Mareva Order.

[
36
]

ORDERS
Defendant
Joseph Feldman and Defendant Khadija El Hachmi
El Alaoui not to, directly or indirectly, mortgage pledge, encumber,
transfer, dispose, cede, assign, sell, transfer, donate, bestow, remove or alienate
in any form, manner or fashion their assets and property wherever situated, in
Canada, the United States of America, Morocco or elsewhere, whether held
directly or indirectly through the intermediary of other persons, whether they
be physical, moral or legal persons, including all representatives as well as
mandated persons, save and except with the prior written consent of Plaintiffs
or this Court.

[
37
]

AUTHORIZES

Defendants Joseph Feldman and Khadija El Hachmi El Alaoui to
spend the equivalent of $5,000 per month towards ordinary
living expenses incurred in the ordinary course, provided that they deliver to
Plaintiffs’ counsel, on a monthly basis, a written statement of such payments,
together with supporting bank records, invoices and receipts.

[
38
]

AUTHORIZES

Defendants to spend a reasonable sum on legal advice and representation not to
exceed $40,000 without authorization of the Court. Before spending any money,
the Defendants must advise the Plaintiffs’ lawyers where the money is to come
from.

[
39
]

AUTHORIZES
Defendants
to agree with the Plaintiffs’ lawyers that the above spending limit should be
increased provided the agreement is in writing or that any assets be used to
make any payment in the ordinary and proper course of business.

[
40
]

ORDERS
Defendants
Joseph Feldman and Khadija El Hachmi El Alaoui to provide Plaintiffs’
lawyers and file in the Court record, within five (5) days of the order to
intervene hereon, with a list of all assets owned or controlled, directly or
indirectly, by any Defendant or by any entity linked to a Defendant and owned
or controlled, directly or indirectly, by such Defendant.

[
41
]

ORDERS
Defendants
Joseph Feldman and Khadija El Hachmi El Alaoui to provide Plaintiffs’
lawyers and file in the Court record, within five (5) days of the order to
intervene hereon, with complete copies of the bank statements (including all
monthly statements and, where applicable, detailed transaction histories) for
the last twelve (12) months for all bank accounts held or used, whether solely
or jointly, in Canada, the United States, Morocco, or elsewhere, by any
Defendant or by any entity linked to a Defendant and owned or controlled,
directly or indirectly, by such Defendant, including all accounts held at any
financial institution.

[
42
]

ORDERS
Defendant Joseph Feldman to provide Plaintiffs’ lawyers
and file in the Court record, within five (5) days of the order to intervene
hereon, written answers under oath to the following questions:

42.1.

Identify each and every bank account, credit union account, brokerage
account, investment account, crypto asset account or wallet, or any other
financial account that you have held or used, alone or jointly, at any time
since January 1, 2025, anywhere in the world, including the name of the
financial institution or platform, the account number, the account holder(s),
and the jurisdiction where the account is maintained.

42.2.

Identify all immovables in which you have held any right or interest,
direct or indirect, at any time since January 1, 2025, whether registered in
your name or held through any corporation, partnership, trust, nominee, or
other intermediaries, including the civic address, the nature of your interest,
and the manner in which title is held.

42.3.

Identify all entities (corporations, partnerships, trusts or other legal
vehicles) that you own or control, directly or indirectly, or for which you are
a director, officer, signing officer, beneficiary, or person with
de facto

control, and describe the nature and extent of your interest in each.

42.4.

In relation to the wire transfer of $2,961,380.89 dated June 21, 2022,
identify the recipient Moroccan financial institution, the recipient account
number/IBAN, and the account holder(s), and state whether any portion of such
funds remains available as of today and, if so, where and in what amount.

42.5.

In relation to the funds transferred on June 21, 2022, identify each
onward movement, withdrawal, conversion, investment, purchase, pledge, or other
disposition of any portion of the funds since June 21, 2022, stating for each
date, amount, destination, and purpose.

42.6.

In relation to the hypothecated loan in the principal amount of
$1,600,000 granted to 2505 2539 Sherbrooke E. Inc., state whether you have
received any payment whatsoever (capital, interest, fees or otherwise) from
2505-2539 Sherbrooke E. Inc. or Mr. Karim Ouellet Zazouh, directly or
indirectly, and if so identify each payment, including the date, amount, payer,
manner of payment, and the account into which it was deposited.

42.7.

Without limiting the foregoing, in relation to the payment you testified
was approximately “$400,000,” state the exact amount, the date(s) received, the
payer(s), the account into which it was deposited, and what was done with those
funds thereafter, including any transfer to Mrs. El Hachmi or to any
account or entity controlled by her.

42.8.

State your current domicile and actual place(s) of residence and
identify any planned relocation in the next six (6) months.

[
43
]

ORDERS
Defendant
Khadija El Hachmi El Alaoui to provide Plaintiffs’ lawyers and file in the
Court record, within five (5) days of the order to intervene hereon, written
answers under oath to the following questions:

43.1.

In relation to the deed of assignment dated October 21, 2022, by
which Joseph Feldman purported to assign to you the hypothecary claim in the
principal amount of $1,600,000.00 granted to 2505-2539 Sherbrooke E. Inc.,
state whether you paid any amount whatsoever to Joseph Feldman (or to any
person or entity for his benefit) as consideration for the Assignment,
including whether you paid $1,600,000.00.

43.2.

If the answer to the foregoing is yes, identify
(i) the exact amount(s) paid (ii) the date(s) of each payment (iii) the manner
of payment (wire transfer, bank draft, cheque, cash or otherwise) (iv) the
financial institution(s) and account number(s) from which the payment(s) were
made, (v) the financial institution(s) and account number(s) to which the
payment(s) were made (including any intermediary accounts), and (vi) the name
of the account holder(s) for each such originating and destination account.

43.3.

In relation to the wire transfer in the amount
of $2,961,380.89 dated June 21, 2022, that was made to a bank account in
Morocco allegedly in your name or under your control, identify (i) the
recipient Moroccan financial institution (ii) the recipient account number
and/or IBAN, and (iii) the name(s) of the account holder(s) and any person(s)
with signing authority or beneficial control over the recipient account.

43.4.

In relation to the transfer in the amount of
$2,961,380.89 dated June 21, 2022, state whether any portion of the transferred
funds remains available or under your control as of today and, if so, specify
(i) the amount (ii) where such funds are currently held (financial institution
and account number/IBAN or other form), and (iii) in whose name the funds are
held.

43.5.

In relation to the funds transferred by way of
the transfer in the amount of $2,961,380.89 dated June 21, 2022, identify each
onward movement, withdrawal, conversion, investment, purchase, pledge, transfer
to any other account or person, or other disposition of any portion of those
funds since June 21, 2022, and for each such transaction state the date,
amount, destination (including the receiving institution and account
number/IBAN where applicable), and purpose.

[
44
]

RESERVES
the
Plaintiffs’ right to examine Defendants Joseph Feldman and Khadija El Hachmi El
Alaoui, in person in Montréal, Québec, Canada, on their assets and statements,
should they fail to (i) produce the documents or (ii) answer the questions set
out the order to intervene hereon.

[
45
]

ORDERS
Defendants
Joseph Feldman and Khadija El Hachmi El Alaoui to provide Plaintiffs’ lawyers
and file in the Court record, within five (5) days of the order to intervene
hereon, with their current domicile address(es).

[
46
]

ORDERS
any person
who gains knowledge of the injunctive orders herein to be made to comply
therewith.

[
47
]

ORDERS
2505-2539
Sherbrooke E. Inc. and Mr. Karim Ouellet Zazouh, upon service of the order, to
refrain from paying, remitting, transferring, or otherwise disbursing any
amount whatsoever, whether capital, interest, fees, settlement proceeds, or
otherwise, that is due or may become due to Joseph Feldman or Khadija El Hachmi
El Alaoui, either personally or through any nominee, until further order of
this Court.

[
48
]

ORDERS
Defendant
Khadija El Hachmi El Alaoui to provide Plaintiffs’ lawyers and file in the
Court record, within five (5) days of the order to intervene hereon, with
complete copies of all exhibits (including any schedules, annexes,
undertakings, counter-letters or other documents) filed or relied upon in
support of her originating application and any subsequent proceedings in
Superior Court file number 500-17-135120-254.

[
49
]

REQUESTS
the
assistance and recognition of any court, tribunal, regulatory or administrative
body anywhere in Canada and of any tribunal or administrative body elsewhere,
in order to give effect to these orders.

[
50
]

DECLARES
good and
valid the presentation delay of the present Application for the Issuance of a
Mareva Order.

[
51
]

ORDERS
the
provisional execution of the judgment to intervene on the present Application
for the Issuance of a Mareva Order, notwithstanding appeal.

[
52
]

DISPENSES
Plaintiffs
from having to furnish a suretyship.

[
53
]

ALLOWS
Plaintiff
to serve the judgment to intervene on the present Application for the Issuance
of a
Mareva
order by all the necessary means, including fax and email,
notwithstanding the restrictions of legal hours and nonlegal days.

[
54
]

DECLARES
that,
for the purposes of service of the order to intervene hereon and any subsequent
order rendered in connection with the present Application for the Issuance of a

Mareva
order, service shall be duly and validly made upon the Defendants
by email transmission of such order(s) to the following email addresses:

54.1.

Defendant Joseph Feldman:
feldman@feldman.team
.

54.2.

Defendant Khadija El Hachmi El Alaoui:

[...]@gmail.com
.

54.3.

Defendants’ counsel, Mtre. Miguel Monroy:
mmonroy@feldmanavocats.com
.

[
55
]

ORDERS
that this
judgment shall remain in effect until 11:59 PM on
April 24, 2026
,
subject to any further renewal(s) thereof;

[
56
]

RESERVES

Defendants’ right to apply to the Court for a modification of those provisions.

[
57
]

THE WHOLE
with
costs against the Defendants.

disponible sous peu, mais considérant que ce délai est de nature à priver les
parties d’une résolution immédiate de leur litige le Tribunal émettra le
présent jugement en langue anglaise, la traduction sera produite au dossier de
la Cour dans les meilleurs délais. En optant pour cette solution, le Tribunal
tient à souligner que dans la présente affaire, il est question d’une
ordonnance qui
ne met pas fin à l’instance
. Une ordonnance dont
l’exécution immédiate est intrinsèque et qui risque de nécessiter la
collaboration d’instances judiciaires aux États-Unis et dans d’autres provinces
canadiennes. Par ailleurs, toutes les procédures étaient rédigées en anglais et
toutes les pièces étaient en langue anglaise.
